related_questions.question: Which vaccines cannot be given together?

text_blocks.snippet: While most vaccines can be given at the same time, there are a few exceptions where timing and spacing are important. Specifically, different pneumococcal vaccines (PCV13 and PPSV23) should not be given together. Additionally, MenACWY-D (Menactra) should not be given at the same time or within 4 weeks of PCV13. For those with certain spleen conditions or HIV, there are also specific considerations regarding the timing of pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines.

list.title: Pneumococcal vaccines:
list.snippet: When both PCV13 and PPSV23 are indicated, PCV13 should be administered first, followed by PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later. If PPSV23 has already been given, wait 8 weeks (for a child) or 1 year (for adults) before giving PCV13.

list.title: Meningococcal vaccine (MenACWY-D) and Pneumococcal vaccine:
list.snippet: In children with functional or anatomic asplenia or HIV, MenACWY-D should not be administered before age 2 to avoid interference with the immune response to PCV13. MenACWY-CRM (Menveo) is the preferred vaccine in this group.

list.title: Live vaccines:
list.snippet: Generally, you can give two live vaccines on the same day, but if you're getting more than two, you should wait four weeks between doses.

list.title: Certain medications:
list.snippet: Some medications, like certain antivirals and antibiotics, can interfere with the effectiveness of specific vaccines. For example, antiviral medications active against varicella zoster virus can reduce the effectiveness of varicella-containing vaccines, and antibiotics can interfere with the oral typhoid and cholera vaccines. It's crucial to consult with a healthcare professional to determine the appropriate timing of vaccines in relation to these medications.
